title: Leaking heating oil tank: what to do next
summary: Recognize residential heating-oil release warning signs, protect people and property, and move to the correct local spill and cleanup route without disturbing the tank.
quickAnswer: Strong petroleum odor, visible oil, fresh staining, sheen, unexplained fuel loss, or seepage changes the job. Avoid ignition sources, do not touch or test the tank, and contact the applicable emergency or spill authority and a qualified response professional.
stateEntryPrompt: Then use your state resource to confirm reporting contacts, cleanup oversight, records, and any homeowner assistance path.
introPoints: Treat an active or suspected release as a safety and environmental response, not a routine removal estimate.
Keep people away from the affected area, remove ignition sources only when it is safe to do so, and avoid spreading the oil.
Use the local fire department or environmental spill contact when an active release or immediate hazard may be present.
whatNotToAssume: Do not open, drain, move, cut, pressure-test, or repair the tank yourself.
Do not wash oil into a drain, soil, sump, or waterway and do not cover the odor with household chemicals.
Do not assume replacing or removing the tank by itself closes reporting, assessment, or cleanup obligations.
bestFor: You smell heating oil, see wet or stained material, find visible oil or sheen, or notice unexplained consumption.
A basement tank, fuel line, outdoor tank, or underground tank may be releasing product.
You need to distinguish immediate response from later inspection, removal, insurance, and documentation work.
beforeYouCall: From a safe location, note the time, odor, visible signs, tank location, and whether oil is moving toward a drain, soil, or water.
Have the property address, heating-oil supplier, tank type if known, and any prior tank or spill records ready.
Ask the responder what immediate containment, reporting, assessment, cleanup, and written documentation are in scope.
documentsThatMatter: Incident or spill numbers, fire-department notes, agency correspondence, and contractor response reports.
Tank, line, soil, groundwater, cleanup, waste-disposal, and laboratory records created during the response.
Insurance notices, invoices, closure documentation, and any agency completion or no-further-action letter.
whenToEscalate: Call emergency services for fire, fumes affecting occupants, a rapidly spreading release, or another immediate danger.
Use a qualified environmental cleanup route when oil has reached soil, a drain, a sump, groundwater, or building materials.
Return to ordinary inspection or replacement planning only after release warning signs have been ruled out.
